description: Hello I'm Jerrick, and alongside my co-founder Reeve, we're two 15 y.o devs building AstroPulse—a health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions. I handle the coding and architecture, driven by my goal of working in cybersecurity. Reeve leads our strategy and aerospace systems planning backed by straight Level 9s in IGCSE, as he works toward a career in aerospace engineering.
summary:
AstroPulse is a real-time spacecraft telemetry and health monitoring web application developed with C#, .NET 10, and Blazor Server, containerized via Docker and deployed on the cloud.

The project addresses the challenge of managing complex aerospace data by providing a dynamic telemetry engine that tracks vital spacecraft metrics, operational statuses, and system alerts through an interactive web interface.

It is important because it bridges the gap between raw backend telemetry and immediate situational awareness, enabling developers and operators to monitor system health, test fault-tolerance scenarios, and visualize simulated deep-space mission data efficiently.
details:
Core Overview & Mission

  • What it is: A real-time web application built to monitor spacecraft health and telemetry on the fly.
  • Core Function: Bridges the gap between raw backend numbers and clear, human-friendly visuals, giving operators and astronauts a fast way to track life-support systems, catch radiation spikes early, and monitor crew health.
  • Emergency Testing: Features built-in simulation controls to test how the system reacts to sudden emergencies like solar particle events or gravity shifts.
  • Mission Impact: Boosts safety and resilience during long deep-space trips, acting as a reliable testing ground for student teams and mission planners to practice emergency drills.

Architecture & Technical Stack

  • Languages: C#, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Frameworks & Runtimes: .NET 10.0, ASP.NET Core, and Blazor Server.
  • Development & Toolchain: Visual Studio, Git, and GitHub.
  • Deployment & Hosting: Docker containerization hosted live on Render.com.

Under the Hood: Telemetry & Design

  • Custom Engine: A deterministic TelemetryEngine refreshes and pushes simulated mission data every 500ms, tracking cabin pressure, habitat temperature, noise levels, radiation flux, and crew vitals.
  • Blazor Server Integration: Delivers fast, low-latency SignalR updates without needing external files or messy data feeds.
  • Holistic Tracking: Blends hard technical engineering with astronaut wellness, combining habitat telemetry with biological tracking (body maps and daily check-ins) into a single dashboard.

Engineering & UX Challenges

  • Performance & Responsiveness: Maintaining a stable, high-performance Blazor Server architecture under continuous, 500ms real-time data streams without memory bloat.
  • User Experience & Clarity: Designing straightforward color-coded threshold alerts (e.g., Caution states at baseline deviations and Critical warnings during sudden pressure drops or radiation spikes) to keep cognitive load low during high-stress scenarios.
  • Cloud Compatibility: Managing the containerization setup (.NET 10 Docker configuration) to ensure smooth, reliable cloud deployment.

Team Considerations & Hardware Scope

  • Framework Trade-off (Blazor Server vs. WebAssembly): The team deliberately chose Blazor Server to maintain heavy computational workloads and state management securely on the backend, ensuring low-latency client rendering without overloading browser memory during prolonged simulations.
  • Refresh Rate vs. Server Memory: We balanced our telemetry loop at a 500ms interval—frequent enough to provide dynamic, realistic life-support fluctuations, yet optimized to prevent excessive SignalR packet overhead.
  • Hardware Context: AstroPulse is structured as a pure software simulation designed for standard mission-control workstations, ruggedized laptops, or habitat tablets, serving as a reliable telemetry interface ready for future integration with physical IoT sensors.
dataRefs: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2 (Human Factors, Habitability, and Environmental Health)
